title: Breaking And Entering: Weyes Blood
summary: Natalie Mering aka Weyes Blood is bringing her doomsday dream-pop to Australia this June. Ahead of her tour and two headlining shows at RISING, Natalie joins Lauren for a wide-ranging conversation on Breaking And Entering.
transcript:
Lauren Taylor spoke with Natalie Mering, who records as Weyes Blood, ahead of her June 2023 Australian tour and two shows at Melbourne's RISING festival. Presented on Breaking and Entering on 25 May 2023, the conversation explores her fifth album, And in the Darkness, Hearts Aglow, the second in a trilogy that began with 2019's Titanic Rising. Mering had previously visited Triple R in February 2020, when she was in Australia for Golden Plains. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: Weyes Blood's music has such a timeless quality, with echoes of '60s folk and '70s West Coast AM radio, and themes that grapple with modern issues like the climate crisis and the difficulty of finding genuine connection for a generation living their lives almost entirely online. Natalie has described 'It's Not Just Me, It's Everybody' as a Buddhist anthem, ensconced in the interconnectivity of all things and the fraying of our social fabric, and that Buddhist idea seems central to the new album. So I began by asking Natalie why it's something she feels so compelled to explore.

Natalie: I think I'm constantly trying to reconcile all the different esoteric interpretations of reality, because I was raised Christian, and Buddhism is kind of like the forbidden fruit for me. Finding the relationship between the cosmology I grew up with and Buddhism, and how that applies to modern thought as well, I just think it's very important and elemental. And if you're going to think about human consciousness, inevitably these are the concepts that are going to come up, because it's still up for debate if we're all actually separate, in my opinion.

Lauren: Finding the light in the darkness can come from human connection as well, and that has always felt like an important theme in your work. But you also explore isolation, chaos and disconnection. The film clip for 'It's Not Just Me, It's Everybody' touches on technology and its role in both connecting and disconnecting us: for those who haven't seen it, you're dancing with an animated cartoon phone that essentially goes around murdering people. But I think you summed it up as —

Natalie: Eating people.

Lauren: Yes. You summed it up as technological cannibalism, harvesting our attention away from each other. How do you find focus and keep healthy tech boundaries in your life? How do you switch off and recharge, especially when you're touring so much?

Natalie: Well, luckily, it doesn't come super naturally to me. I'm right on that weird generational brink where I'm not the biggest social media person, and I don't find a lot of solace, per se, in internet culture, which some friends my age do. So it's kind of a random assignment, I guess, but I just got the Gen X assignment. It doesn't totally resonate with me. But I do feel like it still occupies a lot of my time, and it's kind of how I get news and different things like that. So I just get sick of it. And unfortunately I don't have the same kind of relationship with it that I think a young person does.

Lauren: One book you reference in the letter accompanying the new record is cultural historian Christopher Lasch's The Culture of Narcissism, from 1979, which served as one of the key inspirations for your inquiries into the fragmented nature of our social lives. For those who aren't familiar, can you tell us about the book, and why it inspired this record?

Natalie: The Culture of Narcissism for me was just a cool eye-opener in terms of the myth of Narcissus, which I think we notoriously misinterpret. We think he was so vain that he was obsessed with his own reflection, when in reality he didn't recognise that it was himself. And I think that's something the human race really contends with a lot: we are desperately grasping and searching for something outside of ourselves that will only be accomplished by going within. I think that's what 'God Turn Me Into a Flower' is about, and what people commonly miss about narcissism. Most people talk about the vanity aspect of it, and not the confusion.

Lauren: I know it's an enormous subject, but were you thinking about overcoming narcissism in our modern age?

Natalie: Well, I think the first thing that needs to be overcome in the modern age is that the systems of exchanging information are so disrupted that people don't really know how to talk to each other anymore. There aren't a lot of great public discourse spaces for nuanced conversation. I just sense a difficulty in communicating, and overcoming it would certainly be a healing salve for people to feel more connected to one another, and responsible to one another, and less in their own hall of mirrors. But I do think modern life and modern civilisation cater to a certain degree of isolation, and that is maybe the beginning of the narcissism. Not so much that we're all naturally, inherently narcissistic, taking a bunch of selfies. I think the selfie is a cry for help, you know. So there are things that preclude the narcissistic tendencies, and reasons why we became narcissistic that have their roots many generations back.

Lauren: Those themes of social decay can ultimately be addressed by going beyond selfish ambition and placing more of our focus on community and coming together. What's the importance of community in your life and in the work that you do?

Natalie: I love when I have a community. It means so much to me. It's like a homecoming, because I tend to be more on the rugged individualist side of things, I think as an American, and as a musician who used to travel solo and do a lot of things alone. I do kind of have a lone wolf mentality, and when I find a community of musicians, it's usually kind of a phase. It'll be a certain city I lived in six years ago, and the six months where everybody was just on fire, making a lot of music together and hanging out, or going on a long tour with my crew and my band and really bonding, or making a record. So the community is constantly evolving and shifting around, because I bounce around a lot. I maintain a lone wolf status, but like to engage with communities.

And I will say that over the course of my 11 years or whatever playing music professionally, the community used to be a little more defined, because there was more that people did of their own volition. There was a certain turning point where it became more internet-based, or about trying to go for a piece of the pie, as opposed to setting up DIY shows or house shows, playing with your friends, doing these little crummy tours for nobody, slowly meeting people and building up momentum from just experience. A lot of people nowadays are in the dawn of the death of a lot of DIY venues. It's almost like you have to have a more professional quality right out of the gates. I would say DIY music has been stripped of some of its naivety by the internet: the idea that you could be at a show and it's the centre of the world, because you don't have a phone to show you otherwise.

So the phones, I think, decentralised communities where people used to congregate and meet up. The phones really generate that kind of attitude where you'll be at a show and people will be on their phone, or thinking about somewhere else they could be, and just genuinely a little less engaged. Maybe I'm going to the wrong shows, but this is just something I've noticed. And this is not necessarily for big concerts. When you get to a big concert, everybody really wants to be there. I'm talking about developmental touring, being a nobody band who's just starting out. Those kinds of communities used to be so nourishing and helpful, and I think they're more disparate than they were in the past.

Lauren: Last time you were in Australia, at the very end of February 2020, you came into the Triple R studios to talk about Titanic Rising and its feelings of impending doom, and you told us you were already mentally preparing yourself for an apocalypse, or a terrible thing, at the time of writing that record. Do you feel you were tapping into something that was collectively about to come, a weird premonition?

Natalie: Definitely. I think I have a pretty decent gut instinct that I've been learning about over time, and I could just sense that was the vibe. I think that's maybe how a lot of people felt but didn't know yet. And the pandemic was a bit like truth serum, like gasoline pouring on the fire or something. I've always been a very sensitive person in that way.

Lauren: There was still a hopeful element to Titanic Rising, even an optimistic quality to the word "rising" in the title. You've said it's very important for people to still have hope and not be scared, and that through your work you're trying to shed light on things, comfort people and make sure everyone has each other's backs. How does the new record relate to that, and to its title, And in the Darkness, Hearts Aglow? In the letter accompanying it, you liken your heart to a glow stick that's been cracked, and there's that really powerful image on the cover. Would you describe it as a hopeful record yet? Or, as the second album in a trilogy, where are we at in this phase?

Natalie: I feel like it's kind of the music that was made amidst the blare of the alarm. It's the kind of purgatory where there's no question now that these things are in place and happening. So what does that do to our social fabric, and to our concepts of intimacy, living amongst it, in the thick of it? I find it a little more of an introverted record, more introspective and kind of subterranean in terms of the journey inward.
